assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Potentiometer (potential divider)
items.clue: A resistor with a sliding contact.

items.label: Electric potential difference, V
items.clue: The work done per unit charge in moving charge between two points.

items.label: Electrical resistance, R
items.clue: The ratio of the voltage across a component to the current through it.

questions.stem: A cell has an emf of 1.5 V. What does this mean?

options.text: The cell holds a store of 1.5 C of charge, which it releases into the circuit.
The cell pushes each coulomb of charge around the circuit with a force of 1.5 N.
For each coulomb passing through the cell, 1.5 J is transferred to electrical energy.
The cell drives a current of 1.5 A through any circuit connected to it.

questions.explanation: Emf is the work done by the source per unit charge, ε = W/q, and 1 V = 1 J C⁻¹. So 1.5 J of chemical energy is transferred to electrical energy for every coulomb that the cell moves around the circuit.

questions.stem: A chemical cell and a solar cell are each used as the energy source in a circuit. Which describes the main energy transfer in each?

options.text: Chemical cell: chemical energy to electrical. Solar cell: energy of light to electrical.
Chemical cell: stored electrical energy is let out. Solar cell: light to electrical.
Chemical cell: chemical energy to electrical. Solar cell: the Sun's heat to electrical.
Chemical cell: chemical energy to electrical. Solar cell: its stored light to electrical.

questions.stem: A student wants to measure the current in a lamp and the pd across it, but connects the meters the wrong way round. The circuit is: a cell, a voltmeter and the lamp connected in series in a single loop, with an ammeter connected in parallel with the lamp. Both meters are ideal. What does the student observe?

options.text: The lamp is off and both meters read zero, as there is no current in the circuit.
The lamp is off, the ammeter reads zero and the voltmeter reads the emf of the cell.
The ammeter short-circuits the lamp, so a very large current flows through the ammeter.
The lamp lights normally, and the meters show its current and pd as when correctly connected.

questions.stem: A cell of emf 6.0 V drives a steady current of 0.25 A through a lamp for 2.0 minutes. How much energy does the cell transfer from its chemical store to the charge that passes through it in this time?
questions.explanation: The emf is the energy the cell transfers per coulomb: W = εq. The charge that passes is q = IΔt = 0.25 × 120 = 30 C, so W = 6.0 × 30 = 180 J.

questions.stem: A student writes: 'For a garden lamp that must shine all night, a solar cell is a better energy source than a chemical cell in every way.' Which evaluation of this claim is correct?

options.text: Right: the solar cell stores the energy of the light it absorbs by day and releases it to the lamp at night.
Right: the Sun is a renewable source, so a solar cell gives a steady output at all times, by day or night.
Wrong: a solar cell holds no store of charge, so it cannot drive a current even while light falls on it.
Wrong: sunlight is renewable, but a solar cell gives no output at night, so a storage cell is needed.

questions.stem: Two resistors, each of resistance 100 kΩ, are connected in series across a 6.0 V supply of negligible internal resistance. A voltmeter that is not ideal, with a constant resistance of 100 kΩ, is connected across one of the resistors. What does the voltmeter read?
questions.explanation: The voltmeter's own 100 kΩ is in parallel with the resistor, making 50 kΩ. That 50 kΩ is in series with the other 100 kΩ, so it takes 50/150 of the supply pd: 6.0 × 1/3 = 2.0 V. A non-ideal voltmeter changes the pd it is measuring.

questions.stem: Helium in a cylinder fitted with a piston is a closed system. During one process the piston does 600 J of work on the helium, and the helium loses 400 J of thermal energy to its surroundings. Using Clausius' sign convention, what is the change in internal energy ΔU of the helium?
questions.explanation: Thermal energy is lost, so Q = −400 J; work is done on the gas, so W = −600 J. Q = ΔU + W gives ΔU = Q − W = −400 J − (−600 J) = +200 J. The work done on the gas adds more energy than the heat removes.

questions.stem: Helium, a monatomic ideal gas, is kept at a constant pressure of 1.5 × 10⁵ Pa while it expands from 2.0 dm³ to 5.0 dm³. What is the work W, as it appears in Q = ΔU + W, for this process?
questions.explanation: At constant pressure W = PΔV. ΔV = 5.0 − 2.0 = 3.0 dm³ = 3.0 × 10⁻³ m³, so W = 1.5 × 10⁵ Pa × 3.0 × 10⁻³ m³ = 450 J. It is positive because the gas expands and does work on its surroundings.

questions.stem: A sample of 8.0 g of helium, a monatomic ideal gas of molar mass 4.0 g mol⁻¹, is heated at constant pressure from 20 °C to 80 °C. The thermal energy supplied is 2.49 × 10³ J. R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. What is the change in internal energy ΔU of the helium?
questions.explanation: n = 8.0 g ÷ 4.0 g mol⁻¹ = 2.0 mol and ΔT = 60 K. ΔU = (3/2)nRΔT = 1.5 × 2.0 × 8.31 × 60 = 1.5 × 10³ J. The rest of the 2.5 × 10³ J supplied leaves as work done by the expanding gas.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly relates the entropy of a system to its particles?

options.text: Entropy is the total kinetic energy of all the particles, so it is measured in joules.
Entropy is how untidy the objects in a system look, whatever their particles are doing.
The more ways the particles can be arranged, the greater their disorder and entropy.
Entropy, like energy, is conserved, so the particles keep the same disorder.

questions.explanation: Entropy relates to the degree of disorder of the particles: the more arrangements of positions and energies are consistent with the macrostate, the greater the entropy. This is why a gas has more entropy than the same substance as a liquid or solid.

questions.stem: Helium, a monatomic ideal gas, expands reversibly and isothermally at 27 °C, doing 600 J of work on its surroundings. What is the entropy change of the helium?

options.text: +2.0 J K⁻¹, as Q = W = 600 J is supplied to it at 300 K
0 J K⁻¹, as no heat is transferred at a constant temperature
−2.0 J K⁻¹, as the gas does work, so W = −600 J and Q = −600 J
+22 J K⁻¹, as Q = 600 J is supplied at a temperature of 27 °C

questions.explanation: At constant temperature ΔU = 0 for an ideal gas, so Q = ΔU + W = 600 J of thermal energy is supplied to the helium at T = 300 K. ΔS = ΔQ/T = 600 ÷ 300 = +2.0 J K⁻¹.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a correct statement of the second law of thermodynamics in its Clausius form?

options.text: Thermal energy cannot be moved from a colder body to a hotter body by any means at all.
Thermal energy cannot flow spontaneously from a colder body to a hotter body.
Thermal energy flows spontaneously from the body with more internal energy to the one with less.
Cold flows spontaneously from a colder body into a hotter body until their temperatures are equal.

questions.explanation: This is the Clausius form. The word 'spontaneously' matters: thermal energy can be moved from cold to hot, as in a refrigerator, but only when work is done, so the transfer is not the sole result of the process.
